title: "3. Sensitivities"
---

```{r, include = FALSE, purl = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 96,
                      fig.retina = 2, message = FALSE)
project <- normalizePath("../../examples/oppeltNPJSystBiolAppl2018")
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = project)
knitr::read_chunk("../../examples/oppeltNPJSystBiolAppl2018/sensitivities.R")
library(dMod2)
source("results/stored.R")
```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
s <- stored("results/sensitivities.rds", "sensitivities.R")
```

dMod2 computes derivatives of the objective exactly from the ODE sensitivities and the chain rule
through every function object. Code: `sensitivities.R`; details:
[Methods > Sensitivities and Hessians](methods-sensitivities.html).

`derivMode` of `odemodel()`, `Y()`, `P()` and `Pimpl()` selects the derivatives a function
object is built with: `"forward"`, `"reverse"`, `"forward-forward"`, `"forward-reverse"`, or
`"none"`. The arguments `deriv`, `deriv2` and `sweep` of a call select what the call computes; a
call that asks for a derivative not built is an error.

## Forward sensitivities

The default, `derivMode = "forward"`: `Xs()` integrates $\partial x / \partial \theta$ with the
states, the objective returns gradient and Gauss-Newton Hessian. `sensErrCon` in `optionsSens`
sets whether sensitivities enter the error test (default `TRUE`).

## Forward over forward

`derivMode = "forward-forward"` in `odemodel()`, `Y()`, `P()` and `Pimpl()` builds second-order
sensitivities, and a call with `deriv2 = TRUE` returns the exact Hessian from them. The equation
count grows with the square of the parameters (guide model: `r nrow(s$gradients)`); it suits
small models such as those of
[Nonlinear mixed-effects models](guide-nlme.html).

## Reverse sweep

One backward sweep of the adjoint system gives the gradient at a cost independent of the
parameter count ([Methods > Reverse sweep](methods-sensitivities.html#reverse-sweep)). Build with
`derivMode = c("forward", "reverse")` (`Pimpl()` passes the sweep through the Jacobian of the
root), call with `sweep = "reverse"`. Both passes solve with `options` alone; solves with
sensitivities use `optionsSens` merged over `options`. In
`trust()` the sweep is set per phase:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
fit <- trust(obj, start,
             phases = list(list(hessianMethod = "gn"),
                           list(hessianMethod = "sr1", sweep = "reverse")))
fit$phaseSweep
```

Without `sweep`, `"bfgs"` and `"sr1"` phases sweep backwards if the objective allows it.
Gauss-Newton needs forward sensitivities: a `"gn"` phase with `sweep = "reverse"` is an error.
`"exact"` with `sweep = "reverse"` and `deriv2 = TRUE` uses forward over reverse.

The backward sweep follows the step grid of the value pass by default; on the cppDE backend
`optionsReverse` of `Xs()` sets the accuracy, see `cppDE::adjointControl()`:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
x <- Xs(model, options = list(atol = 1e-8, rtol = 1e-6),
        optionsReverse = list(refine = TRUE, gradtol = 1e-3))
controls(x, name = "optionsReverse") <- list(refine = FALSE)   # the grid of the value pass again
```

| entry | controls |
|---|---|
| `refine` | `TRUE`: each sweep step passes the error test of the solve, else is redone in substeps |
| `gradtol` | absolute tolerance for the share of each step in the gradient |

Under `refine`, value and `chi2` include the change to the refined trajectory, attribute
`correction`
([Methods > Accuracy of a reverse gradient](methods-sensitivities.html#accuracy-of-a-reverse-gradient)).

## Forward over reverse

The exact Hessian without second-order sensitivities, one column per parameter
([Methods > Forward over reverse](methods-sensitivities.html#forward-over-reverse)). Build with
`derivMode = c("forward", "reverse", "forward-reverse")`, call with
`sweep = "reverse", deriv2 = TRUE`. FOCEI in [Nonlinear mixed-effects models](guide-nlme.html)
uses it for directional second derivatives.

## ODE backends

`odemodel(backend = )` selects the solver:

| backend | solver | forward | fwd/fwd | reverse | fwd/rev | use |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `"cppDE"` (default) | C++: BDF/NDF, Adams, Rosenbrock, Tsitouras | duals | duals | discrete adjoint | yes | all models |
| `"Sundials"` | CVODES, `cppDE::cvode()` | CVODES | no | CVODES ASA | no | first-order derivatives |
| `"deSolve"` | `lsodes`, cOde | sens. equations | no | no | no | dMod models |

cppDE on [stepping](https://dmodverse.github.io/cppDE/articles/methods-stepping.html),
[CVODES](https://dmodverse.github.io/cppDE/articles/methods-cvode.html) and
[benchmarks](https://dmodverse.github.io/cppDE/articles/benchmarks.html) against CVODES.

## Costs on the guide model

`sensitivities.R` evaluates the data term of [Setting up models](guide-model.html) at the best
fit of [Optimization](guide-optimization.html); the results are loaded from
`results/sensitivities.rds`.

```{r reversechain, eval = FALSE}
```

```{r}
s <- readRDS("results/sensitivities.rds")
```

Relative difference of reverse and forward gradient:

```{r gradients, eval = FALSE}
```

```{r}
max(abs(s$gradients$forward - s$gradients$reverse)) / max(abs(s$gradients$forward))
```

Seconds per evaluation, minimum of ten:

```{r cost, eval = FALSE}
```

```{r}
s$timing
```

Forward over reverse costs about
`r round(s$timing[["forward-reverse"]] / s$timing[["forward"]], 1)` forward gradients; forward over
forward, once:

```{r forwardforward, eval = FALSE}
```

```{r}
c(seconds = s$forwardForward, s$memory)
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
peakText <- if (s$memory[["forwardForward"]] > s$memory[["before"]] + 0.05) {
  sprintf("raises the peak memory of the process from %.1f to %.1f GB", s$memory[["before"]],
          s$memory[["forwardForward"]])
} else sprintf("leaves the peak memory of the process at %.1f GB", s$memory[["before"]])
```

It takes `r round(s$forwardForward / s$timing[["forward-reverse"]])` times as long as forward
over reverse and `r peakText`. Relative difference of the two Hessians:

```{r hessians, eval = FALSE}
```

```{r}
max(abs(s$forwardForwardHessian[rownames(s$exact), colnames(s$exact)] - s$exact)) / max(abs(s$exact))
```

Eigenvalues of exact and Gauss-Newton Hessian at the best fit:

```{r, fig.height = 3.5}
eig <- data.frame(rank = rep(seq_len(nrow(s$hessians)), 2),
                  value = c(s$hessians$exact, s$hessians$gaussNewton),
                  Hessian = rep(c("exact", "Gauss-Newton"), each = nrow(s$hessians)))
ggplot2::ggplot(eig, ggplot2::aes(rank, value, color = Hessian)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point() +
  ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(trans = scales::pseudo_log_trans(sigma = 1e-3, base = 10),
                              breaks = c(-1e-1, 0, 1e-2, 1, 1e2, 1e4)) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "rank", y = "eigenvalue") +
  theme_dMod2()
```

The smallest eigenvalue is `r signif(min(s$hessians$exact), 2)` for the exact Hessian and
`r signif(min(s$hessians$gaussNewton), 2)` for Gauss-Newton.

Reference: `odemodel()`, `Xs()`, `Y()`, `P()`, `Pimpl()`, `normL2()`, `controls()`, `trust()`
